h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר י׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Yud

p: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him:
for the ransom of the soul
is not repayment of a debt they borrowed,
The matter is based on what is written
there is no strength like the strength of piety at its beginning.
And they said in the name of the Rebbe, Reb Bunim,
may the memory of the holy tzaddik be a blessing,
כִּי לֹא מֵחָכְמָה שָׁאַלְתָּ עַל זֶה
for it is not out of wisdom that you ask about this";
that is, the strength of piety
did not come from your own wisdom,
but through a loan and a borrowing
so that he attain it through his own toil.
may the memory of the holy tzaddik be a blessing, said
that a person is shown at his beginning
only as much as he will be able to attain
And at the Splitting of the Sea
there was the aspect of seeing,
a maidservant saw at the Sea
the light was fixed as a lasting acquisition
According to what has been said,
like the repayment of a debt
מַה שֶּׁזָּכוּ בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף בִּשְׁאֵלָה
for what they had merited at the Splitting of the Sea on loan;
better that she be judged as an unmarried woman, etc. —
what they took as a loan and a borrowing
at Pesach and the Splitting of the Sea;
and about this it says "Ki sisa,"
"Through what is the horn of Yisrael raised?
this is called repaying what they borrowed,
since they merit the raising of the horn
that there be the unity of "echad,"
which indicates that the aleph and ches,
the nine attributes, shine in the dalet —
the heh was a dalet, etc. —
and the light is fixed as a lasting acquisition;
they repay the loan and the borrowing,
since the blemish of the Calf has been rectified.
And on every Shabbos, at the third meal,
as written in Sefer Mateh Moshe
that for this reason we say at Minchah
they merit to bring "zeh" close to "zos,"
זוֹכִין לְיִחוּד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵּיהּ
they merit the unity of Kudsha Brich Hu and His Shechinah,
"in the light of the King's face is life."
"And the number of Bnei Yisrael shall be," etc.,
"it shall be said to them, children of the living G-d" —
that is, as it was at Matan Torah.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 39:1 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: Israel owe Me what they borrowed from Me, as it says, ‘Ki sisa,’ like the expression, ‘When you lend to your fellow.’ Tell them to repay what they owe Me: this is ki sisa. Then I will make payment to them, as it says, ‘The number of the children of Israel will be like the sand of the sea.’” The Midrash deliberately reads the census word sisa through the language of lending, tasheh. Its closing promise is Hoshea 2:1, the verse to which Rav Tzadok returns at the maamar’s end.

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaRokeach, Introduction — “There is no strength like the strength of piety at its beginning.” The maxim appears among a sequence praising truthfulness, a good heart, standing firm under trial, remembrance of the Creator, and the flame of awe. The explanation of that initial strength as a loan, and the ensuing application to the first and acquired stages of revelation, are the Chassidic interpretation presented by Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach 1 — “This light is only for the moment, so that a person see that there is the light of His G-dliness in the world; afterward it is hidden from him, and he sees all he has done against Hashem’s will… his heart breaks and he returns in complete teshuvah.” Rav Tzadok there explains what the withdrawal of the borrowed light produces: the broken heart through which one earns it by one’s own toil.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShemesh, Yisro, s.v. Vayesapper Moshe (digital paragraph 5) — “At a person's first awakening to repentance, the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him an exceedingly great illumination, so that a very great awakening comes upon him. This is ‘He gives a hand to transgressors.’ But this illumination is immediately forgotten and concealed from him, so that he will search and investigate for himself through Torah, prayer, and good deeds, through choice and will. The further a person advances in service, the more there is revealed to him of what the Creator, blessed be He, illuminated for him at that first glimpse. This is the statement in Sefer Rokeach that there is no strength in piety like its beginning: at the beginning of piety the Holy One shows him a great illumination, but afterward it is concealed from him, until he must seek it out diligently to return to that first piety with which he began. In the writings this is called the first state of greatness: the Holy One illuminates of Himself to clarify His divinity. Afterward the person enters smallness of mind, when that first understanding is concealed, and then great effort is required to attain the former understanding and the yearning he had at the beginning. … Because Israel had possessed great clarity on the first night, whenever they fell they recalled that first great clarity—the strength of piety at the beginning. This sustained them, enabling them to awaken themselves whenever they fell and return to their original faith, until they came to the giving of the Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Maor VaShemesh explains the same Rokeach maxim through the distinction between an illumination given from above and one recovered through freely chosen service. Its continuing effect is the remembered clarity that sustains the search during concealment; the passage applies this process to Israel's journey from the Exodus to Sinai. This supplies a concrete account of Rav Tzadok's “loan”: withdrawal creates the work through which the original gift can become an acquired possession. Rav Tzadok further explains the shekalim as repairing the calf's interruption of that acquisition.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 13 — “At the sea, though Atika was revealed, it was only as seeing, showing them what they could attain at Shavuos through acquisition… our holy Rebbe said the seeing at the sea was like the strength of piety at its beginning.” There Rav Tzadok adds that this is why chametz is forbidden on Pesach yet brought in the Shavuos loaves: only once the light is acquired is the yetzer subdued.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 43:1 — “A ruler sent a matchmaker to betroth a woman. She went astray with another man. What did the matchmaker do? He took the marriage document he had been given and tore it. He said: Better that she be judged as unmarried than as a married woman. So Moshe acted when Israel did that deed: He took the tablets and broke them. He said: Had they seen the punishment written in them, they would not have sinned. It is better that they be judged as inadvertent sinners rather than deliberate ones.” Breaking the tablets is portrayed as the intermediary’s defense of Israel after the calf. Rav Tzadok invokes the interrupted marriage to explain why the earlier illumination remained an unpaid loan.

paragraphs.text: Mateh Moshe 482, Shabbos Minchah — “Israel and Shabbos testify concerning the Holy One, blessed be He, that He is One and all was made by His word, and that He sanctifies Israel and Shabbos. The Holy One, blessed be He, and Shabbos testify concerning Israel that they are treasured above all peoples, holy, and one nation on earth. It is fitting for the One God to unite with one nation on one distinguished day. Therefore at Shabbos Minchah one says, ‘You are One.’” The original siman 482 is embedded within the digital site’s reflowed chapter 99. It explains the unity expressed by the Minchah prayer through the reciprocal testimony of Hashem, Israel and Shabbos. The maamar connects this time with the third meal.
